blocks.text: Billy had said to meet him outside the building with the blue doors.
Seth looked up at the tall windows. Then he looked down at the address Billy had written on a scrap of paper.
“This one?”
Jenny leaned over his shoulder. “Unless there's another enormous blue door behind us.”

They had come in their suits. Seth straightened his red mask while Jenny checked the street, her blonde curls lifting in the breeze. A small truck rattled past the red-brick building and turned toward the warehouses.
Billy waited beneath the entrance lamp with Fist on a folded cushion across his arms. Beside him stood Claude Blackwell, smiling as though he had been waiting all morning to show them something.
Eleanor stood a little apart in her black suit and dark glasses.
Seth slowed.
Claude came forward before he could think of anything to say.
blocks.alt: Claude welcomes costumed Seth and Jenny at the facility’s blue doors while Billy supports injured Fist on a cushion and Eleanor stands apart.

blocks.text: “I'm glad you could come.” He held up a ring of keys. “Billy tells me you've been practicing on a roof.”
“It has a good view,” Jenny said.
“And an edge,” Billy said.
“Several,” Seth admitted.
Claude looked back at the building. “I thought we might improve on that.”
He unlocked the blue doors and held one open.

Inside, the entrance hall smelled of fresh paint. Sunlight fell through tall windows onto a floor that had recently been polished. To the left, another pair of doors stood open on a broad room with blue mats.
Seth stopped on the threshold.
There was space to run. Space to turn around. Space between the equipment and the walls.
He stepped onto a mat and pressed down with one boot.
“Is this for us?”
“For the Defenders,” Claude said. “Yes.”

Jenny walked a little farther into the room. Thick crash mats stood stacked at one side. A heavy bag hung in a clear corner. Weights waited on a rack, and a target plate stood against a high brick wall at the far end.
She looked up. The ceiling was high enough that Seth followed her gaze and began smiling.
“No experiments today,” Billy said.
“I hadn't said anything.”
“You were looking.”
Claude laughed. “We'll have somebody go through the equipment with you. Anything unsuitable, tell me. I'd rather have it changed than have you make do.”
Seth walked back across the mats, testing the spring beneath his feet.
“Why?” he asked.
Claude looked at him.
“All this,” Seth said. “Why are you giving it to us?”
“I've been reading the paper.”
Jenny glanced at Billy. He was watching Claude, too.
“You keep turning up when people need you,” Claude said. “I thought you ought to have somewhere to come back to.”
Eleanor adjusted the bracelet at her wrist.
“Claude has taken a considerable interest,” she said.
“I have,” he agreed, and led them toward the next room.
The operations room had more screens than Seth had ever seen together outside a shop window.

Beige computers sat along a broad desk. One showed green letters against black. Beside them, a bank of smaller television monitors displayed the entrance, a side door and the loading area. Wires ran neatly into channels behind the desks.
Jenny pulled up a chair and bent toward a keyboard without touching it.
“Do these all work?”
Claude nodded. “There's somebody coming to show you how to use them. Manuals are in the drawers.”
She opened one. It was full.
“Quite a lot to show us,” she said.
Billy had already noticed the cameras.
“Those are outside?”
“On this building,” Claude said. “Front, side and loading door. The recorders are underneath.”
Billy crouched to look at the video decks. Fist leaned over the cushion's edge.
blocks.alt: Claude shows the Defenders the 1987 operations room, with beige computers, wired entrance-camera monitors and video recorders; Billy carries Fist on his cushion.

blocks.text: “What happens if I wave at one?”
“You appear on television,” Jenny told him.
Fist considered that. “Good equipment.”
There were telephones, a street map and an empty rack for folders. At the end of the desk sat a radio with a row of buttons, a tuning knob and a narrow display.
Billy went straight to it.
“Police-band scanner,” he said.
“I asked what would be useful,” Claude replied. “That was on the list.”
Billy set Fist's cushion on a clear section of desk. He checked that the torn cuff was supported, then turned the scanner on.
Static filled the room.
Fist opened one eye. “Very useful.”
Billy adjusted the volume and worked the controls. A voice came through, broke into a hiss, then returned.
He leaned nearer, turning the knob a little farther.
blocks.alt: Billy tunes the police-band scanner while Seth, Jenny and Eleanor listen; Fist rests beside him on a cushion with his torn cuff supported.

blocks.text: The voice became clear enough for them to hear a dispatcher send a car to a stalled vehicle holding up traffic.
Billy stopped touching the controls.
Everyone listened until another voice acknowledged the call.
Seth looked at the map on the wall. “That's only a few streets from here.”
“It receives,” Billy said. “We listen. We don't get on it and start giving orders.”
Fist settled again. “I hadn't even started.”
Billy found a pencil beside a fresh pad and wrote down the street, then checked the map. Jenny watched him do it.
“You look at home already,” she said.
Billy glanced around the desk. “There's room for the notebook.”
“There is an entire library upstairs,” Claude said.
Billy put down the pencil.

The library overlooked part of the training room from a broad mezzanine. Shelves lined the walls, with books on science, engineering, Cleveland and enough other subjects that Seth stopped trying to read every spine.
Maps filled a shallow cabinet. At the center stood a large wooden table, several lamps and chairs that did not have anyone's coat hanging over them yet.
Billy pulled out one chair and tested it.
Jenny took a book from the local-history shelf, opened it and showed him a page. Within a minute they were both leaning over it.
Claude waited with a pleased expression.
Eleanor looked down into the training room.
“You've certainly thought of everything,” she said.
“Not quite.” Claude turned toward Fist, who was still on his cushion in Billy's arms. “There's something else.”
They went back downstairs and along a short corridor. A small sitting area had a sofa, a low table and a counter with a kettle. Beyond it stood a row of blue lockers.
Claude stopped before one with a brass nameplate.
FIST-O-MITE.
Fist stared at it.
“For your things,” Seth suggested.
“What things?”
Claude opened the door.

A broad shelf had been fitted inside at a comfortable height. On it lay a deep blue cushion, with a folded blanket at one end. There was room above it for Fist to sit upright without striking the shelf overhead.
Fist looked from the cushion to Claude.
“It's for sleeping?”
“If you'd like it.”
Billy brought him closer. Fist shifted forward, moved carefully from one cushion to the other, and settled with his damaged cuff resting on the soft edge.
Nobody spoke while he tested it.
He turned a little, then a little farther. He looked up at his nameplate on the open door.
“Don't shut that.”
“We won't,” Claude said.
Fist sank into the cushion.
“This one stays here?”
“It belongs to you.”
Seth felt Jenny's hand find his. He looked at her, and she smiled without saying anything.
“Thank you,” Fist said.
Claude bent a little so they were closer to eye level. “You're very welcome.”
blocks.alt: Fist settles into his cushioned blue sleeping locker while Claude bends beside him, Billy holds the carrying cushion, and Seth and Jenny smile together.

blocks.text: Eleanor's hand tightened around the clasp of her handbag. By the time Claude straightened, she had loosened it.
“We should let them look around,” she said.
“Of course.” Claude held out the keys to Billy. “I'll have the instructions brought over. And the people to explain the equipment. You have my number if something needs attention.”
Billy looked down at the keys in his palm.
“I don't know what to say.”
“You've said thank you. That's plenty.”
At the doors, Eleanor paused beside Billy.
“Try to keep the place in one piece.”
“We intend to,” he said.
Claude was already looking up at the windows, pleased with how the light fell through them. Eleanor followed him out. She had said very little about the Defenders themselves.
Seth watched the blue door close.
“Are we really allowed to stay?”
Billy lifted the keys.
Jenny laughed, and the sound carried into the training room.

They went back inside. Billy returned to the operations desk and began reading the scanner instructions. Jenny brought down a street atlas from the library. Seth found the cups beside the kettle and counted them twice before putting them on the counter.
From the locker alcove, Fist called, “I can still hear you.”
“Good,” Billy said. “We're putting the kettle on.”
Seth stood in the corridor a moment longer. There were people in the rooms on either side of him, making plans and opening drawers. He knew where they would be tomorrow.
Farther along the lake, Laura Baxter heard a soft sound above the water and looked up.
A small orange light was moving toward her.
She got to her feet, pushing her glasses straight. For an instant she thought something else was falling from the sky.
The light slowed.
There was a face inside it.
Laura backed away from the rocks. Flaming Head stopped well short of her, with the water behind him and the empty path between them.
“Please don't come closer,” she said.
“I won't.”
She stared at him. The words had reached her as clearly as if someone had spoken beside her ear, but there was nobody there.
“Did you say that?”
“Yes.”
She looked along the path. No one was coming.
Flaming Head stayed where he was.
“I think you've been asking for help.”
blocks.alt: On the lakeside path at dusk, Laura in glasses, gray sweatpants and a dark jacket faces Flaming Head, who hovers at a respectful distance above the shoreline rocks.

blocks.text: Laura's fingers tightened around the edge of her jacket.
“You heard me?”
“I felt that someone needed me. I came to look.”
For a moment, she could not answer. He was still there when she managed to speak.
“Something happened to me. In the water.”
“I know something about that.”
Laura took a careful breath. She had explained it in offices and bathrooms and once to her own reflection. This time the person listening had come to find her.
“Can you make it stop?”
